subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Why Insurance Feels Worth It
description: One-minute skill: Why Insurance Feels Worth It.

hook.text: You pay $1,200 a year for insurance you'll probably never use. On paper it's a loss. It still feels worth it.

buildup.text: Insurance eliminates a small probability of a huge loss. The possibility effect inflates the fear of that loss.

discovery.text: We're paying to remove dread, not to optimize expected value. Peace of mind has its own price tag.

twist.text: Extended warranties exploit this. The chance of breakdown is tiny, but the pain of losing a new phone feels huge.

climax.text: Ask: can I absorb this loss? If yes, you're paying for emotion, not protection. Sometimes that's fine. Know it.

quiz.question: Why do people overpay for insurance against rare events?
options: Insurance companies set prices too low
We overweight small probabilities of big losses
Rare events are actually very common

details.summary: Insurance feels worth its cost because the possibility effect overweights small probabilities of catastrophic loss, and loss aversion makes the potential devastation feel psychologically unbearable even when actuarially unlikely.
details.whyItMatters: Insurance is a product where most buyers pay more than they ever claim. Prospect theory explains why this feels rational: the peace of mind from eliminating a dreaded possibility is worth the certain cost of premiums.
takeaways: Small probabilities of large losses are psychologically overweighted
Eliminating even a tiny risk provides disproportionate peace of mind
Insurance converts dreaded uncertain losses into tolerable certain costs

faq.question: Why do people over-insure against unlikely events?
faq.answer: The combination of the possibility effect inflating the perceived probability and loss aversion amplifying the perceived pain of the possible loss makes even unlikely catastrophes feel intolerable. Insurance eliminates this psychological burden entirely.

faq.question: Is buying insurance irrational from an economic standpoint?
faq.answer: By expected value, paying premiums that exceed expected claims is a losing bet. But prospect theory shows it is psychologically rational because eliminating a dreaded uncertainty provides value that pure mathematics cannot capture.
